title: Google takes Dreambeans to India in bid to bring AI-generated personal stories to the masses
author: Jagmeet Singh
contentSnippet:
Google has launched its experimental AI app Dreambeans in India, its first market outside the U.S., as the company looks to tap the world’s second-largest internet market to bring personalized visual stories drawn from users’ digital activity to a broader audience.

On Monday, Google expanded Dreambeans, available on Android and iOS, to India with support for 13 local languages, including Hindi, Punjabi, Tamil, Telugu, and Bengali, alongside English. The launch comes less than two months after Google made the app available to all eligible U.S. users aged 18 and older.

Introduced in June, Google’s Dreambeans uses information from connected Google services, including Calendar, Gemini, Gmail, Photos, Search, and YouTube, to proactively generate personalized, illustrated stories about users’ interests and everyday lives, without requiring them to enter a prompt. The app initially featured static, AI-generated illustrations, but Google recently added a feature that uses its Veo video-generation model to even animate images in select stories.

Google said it chose India as Dreambeans’ first international market because of strong interest from Indian users seeking access to the app and the widespread use of its services in the country. India stood out for its high overlap of users across Gemini, Gmail, and Google Photos, Google product manager Gozde Oznur said during a press briefing.

Dreambeans has recorded nearly 55,000 downloads in the U.S. since its June debut, according to estimates from market intelligence firm Sensor Tower shared with TechCrunch. About 63% of those downloads came in September, when Google opened the app to all eligible U.S. users aged 18 and older. However, downloads dropped 84% month over month to about 5,500 in October.

In the first 30 days after Google opened Dreambeans to all eligible U.S. users, the app recorded an estimated 29,000 downloads, compared with 7.4 million for Meta’s Muse, 2.8 million for ChatGPT, 362,000 for Grok Bot, and 155,000 for Claude during their respective first 30 days after launch, Sensor Tower estimates show. However, unlike those general-purpose AI apps, Dreambeans focuses on generating personalized stories instead of responding to a broad range of user queries.

Even though Dreambeans supports many widely spoken Indian languages, users can select only one language at a time for their generated stories. The a

summary.tldr:
Google has expanded its experimental AI application, Dreambeans, to India, marking the product's first international launch outside the United States. Available on Android and iOS, the app utilizes Google’s 'Personal Intelligence' technology to synthesize data from connected services—including Gmail, Calendar, Photos, Search, and YouTube—to generate personalized, illustrated stories without requiring manual user prompts. The Indian release supports 13 local languages, including Hindi, Bengali, Telugu, Tamil, and Punjabi, alongside English, though the app currently restricts output to a single language at a time, preventing the generation of 'Hinglish' or mixed-language narratives.

Technically, Dreambeans leverages static AI-generated illustrations and has integrated Google’s Veo video-generation model to animate select story segments. According to Sensor Tower data, the app recorded approximately 55,000 U.S. downloads since its June debut, with a significant drop-off in October (5,500 downloads) compared to September (34,650 downloads). While the app is positioned as a personalized storytelling tool rather than a general-purpose chatbot, its adoption metrics remain significantly lower than competitors like ChatGPT or Meta’s Muse. Google product manager Gozde Oznur noted that the app is restricted to personal Gmail accounts and excludes enterprise users, with privacy controls allowing users to disconnect specific services or delete data from the personalization system.
takeaways: **Language Support:** The app supports 13 Indian languages but cannot currently process or generate mixed-language content, such as Hinglish.
**Technical Integration:** Dreambeans utilizes Google's Veo model for video animation and 'Personal Intelligence' for cross-service data synthesis.
**Adoption Metrics:** Sensor Tower estimates show 55,000 total U.S. downloads since June, with a sharp 84% month-over-month decline in October.
**Privacy Controls:** Users can opt out of specific Google services, delete personal data, and instruct the app to avoid sensitive subjects, such as business-related information or specific memories.

title: VCs bet $30M on Larridin’s ability to help enterprises demonstrate AI’s value for money
author: Mike Wheatley
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 21:12 EST / NOVEMBER 02 2026

VCs bet $30M on Larridin’s ability to help enterprises demonstrate AI’s value for money

As enterprises jack up their spending on artificial intelligence tools, it’s only right for senior executives to want to know exactly what they’re getting in return for their costly investments. Larridin Inc. , a startup focused on AI adoption measurement, has just raised $30 million in early-stage funding to try to provide them with the answers.

Today’s Series A round was led by Pelion Ventures and saw participation from existing backers Andreessen Horowitz and Gradient Ventures, as well as new investors like GFT, W23, Thayer, DG Daiwa Ventures, Cougar Capital and Alumni Ventures. The round brings the company’s total amount raised so far to $47 million.

Larridin’s funding comes at a time when enterprise leaders are facing growing pressure to demonstrate the value they’re getting for their spiralling token consumption costs and application programming interface bills. Shareholders of publicly traded companies, especially, are eager to see those investments are driving real growth, and aren’t easily swayed by vanity metrics showcasing adoption without value.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Russ Fradin says this pressure stems from the flawed way in which most organizations evaluate their AI investments. He argues that traditional adoption metrics such as seat licenses and login counts do not reflect the true operational impact of AI.

Indeed, one of Larridin’s own customers is a case in point. That organization’s own surveys showed that 92% of its engineers were active AI users, which seems like a good rate of adoption. But when it started using Larridin’s tools to dig deeper, it found that a single engineer accounted for 65% of the company’s entire AI budget.

These aren’t the only kinds of blind spots AI has created. In Larridin’s newly released Engineering AI Impact Report , based on a survey of more than 1,000 developers, it found that though AI-assisted pull requests increased from 35% in April to 62% in September, it didn’t provide much value for enterprises because it simply created bottlenecks further downstream. For instance, organization’s median code review wait times increased more than 50% over the same timeframe.

Fradin says this is why companies cannot just monitor AI output volume. What’s needed is a complete pictur

summary.tldr:
Enterprise AI adoption measurement startup Larridin Inc. has secured $30 million in a Series A funding round led by Pelion Ventures, bringing its total capital raised to $47 million. Additional participants in the round include existing backers Andreessen Horowitz and Gradient Ventures, alongside new investors GFT, W23, Thayer, DG Daiwa Ventures, Cougar Capital, and Alumni Ventures. Co-founded by Chief Executive Russ Fradin, the company aims to address enterprise pressures regarding spiraling token consumption costs and API billing by offering what it describes as the industry's first AI value measurement platform.

Larridin's platform links AI tool adoption data with employee productivity metrics and expenditure tracking, addressing flaws in traditional vanity metrics such as seat licenses and login counts. According to data from the company's Engineering AI Impact Report—which surveyed over 1,000 developers—AI-assisted pull requests rose from 35% in April to 62% in September, yet median code review wait times increased by over 50% due to downstream bottlenecks. The platform also evaluates autonomous AI agent costs and output quality, having previously uncovered blind spots such as a single engineer consuming 65% of an organization's AI budget despite a 92% active usage rate, and a 66-fold cost discrepancy per shipped code change between competing coding tools.

The newly acquired capital will be deployed to expand Larridin's engineering and go-to-market teams. The startup's current enterprise customer roster includes SurveyMonkey Inc., Vertiv Holdings Co., Klaviyo Inc., and Gainsight Inc.
takeaways: **Funding Details:** Larridin Inc. raised a $30 million Series A round led by Pelion Ventures, bringing its total funding to $47 million with participation from Andreessen Horowitz, Gradient Ventures, GFT, W23, Thayer, DG Daiwa Ventures, Cougar Capital, and Alumni Ventures.

**Developer Productivity Bottlenecks:** Larridin's Engineering AI Impact Report revealed that while AI-assisted pull requests grew from 35% in April to 62% in September, median code review wait times increased by more than 50% over the same period.

**Cost Discrepancies Identified:** The platform helped a customer discover a 66-fold cost discrepancy per shipped code change between two competing AI coding tools used for similar tasks, allowing the company to cancel the expensive subscription without productivity loss.

**Usage Asymmetry:** In one customer case study cited by Larridin, an organization reported 92% active engineer usage, but deeper analysis showed that a single engineer accounted for 65% of the company's total AI budget.
**Enterprise Customers:** Larridin's existing client base includes SurveyMonkey Inc., Vertiv Holdings Co., Klaviyo Inc., and Gainsight Inc.

title: Apple may try to increase revenue by doing…something with third-party AI apps
author: Lucas Ropek
contentSnippet:
Apple’s services business remains at record levels, but it’s facing growing pressure . The central part of that business, Apple’s App Store, has faced regulatory pressure and a slump in mobile gaming, which have hurt services growth .

However, on Monday’s earnings call, Apple signaled that it may look to boost services revenue through third-party apps. What does that mean, exactly? Unfortunately, it’s not entirely clear.

When discussing how AI could potentially “contribute to revenue growth over time,” Kevan Parekh, Apple’s chief financial officer, said: “On the product side, you know, we feel AI offers a compelling reason for customers to upgrade and switch in order to get the latest capabilities, and we also feel there’s opportunities across third-party apps and partnerships as well as first-party opportunities.”

Parekh did not elaborate on what sorts of opportunities might be available via third-party apps. However, Reuters reported Monday that investors are wondering whether Apple could profit by distributing third-party AI agents through the App Store and taking a cut of the revenue they generate.

Regulatory and legal changes have cut into App Store commission revenue in some markets, even as Apple’s services business as a whole continues to grow. Third-party estimates in August, for example, suggested the company had seen an 18% drop in U.S. commission revenue, with declines also in Brazil and Japan after those countries introduced new regulations. Apple has traditionally controlled payments within its app marketplace tightly, taking a cut of all App Store transactions. But a lawsuit by Epic Games ultimately forced the company to allow apps to redirect users to outside payment systems. Other legal challenges throughout the world have further hampered the business.

During the earnings call, Parekh referenced Apple’s App Store woes and returned to the idea that the company’s service business could expand into new territory.

“We’ve also seen some factors that impacted the performance of the App Store, and during the September quarter, the performance on the App Store was similar to the prior year, and we had a record number of paid subscriptions with double-digit growth for third-party apps on the App Store,” Parekh said. “At the same time, we did see some headwinds in mobile gaming that we’ve talked about before, and expect to see those continue in

summary.tldr:
Apple CFO Kevan Parekh signaled during the company's latest earnings call that Apple is exploring new revenue streams through third-party AI applications and partnerships. While specific implementation details remain undisclosed, the company views AI as a primary driver for hardware upgrade cycles and a potential catalyst for services growth. Investors are speculating that this could involve Apple distributing third-party AI agents via the App Store and capturing a commission on the revenue generated by these services.

This strategic pivot comes as Apple faces significant regulatory and legal headwinds impacting its traditional App Store commission model. The company reported an 18% drop in U.S. commission revenue as of August, exacerbated by international regulatory changes in Brazil and Japan and the fallout from the Epic Games litigation, which forced Apple to permit alternative payment systems. Despite these challenges, Apple reported record numbers of paid subscriptions and double-digit growth for third-party apps, even as mobile gaming performance continues to stagnate. Apple projects services growth for the December quarter to be between 8% and 9%, a forecast that accounts for ongoing headwinds in third-party licensing and foreign exchange fluctuations.
takeaways: **Revenue Outlook:** Apple projects services growth between 8% and 9% for the December quarter, factoring in sequential headwinds from third-party licensing.
**Regulatory Impact:** Apple experienced an 18% decline in U.S. App Store commission revenue as of August, driven by global regulatory shifts and the Epic Games legal ruling.
**Growth Drivers:** CFO Kevan Parekh identified AI as a key incentive for consumer hardware upgrades and a potential area for new third-party app partnerships.
**Market Headwinds:** The company continues to face a slump in mobile gaming, which Apple expects to persist through the upcoming summer quarter.

title: How Xatoms is using AI to solve the global water crisis
author: Zeus Kerravala
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 20:49 EST / NOVEMBER 02 2026

How Xatoms is using AI to solve the global water crisis

Every September, Climate Week and Global Citizen Week in New York bring together policymakers, investors and innovators focused on the world’s most pressing problems.

It’s also when Cisco Systems Inc. and Global Citizen recognize the winner of the Global Citizen Prize: Cisco Youth Leadership Award . Cisco and Global Citizen created the award in 2018 to honor a young leader who uses technology to help end extreme poverty, and this year’s recipient may have the most compelling story yet.

Diana Virgovicova (pictured) is the founder and CEO of Xatoms (pronounced “X-Atoms”), a Toronto-based company that uses artificial intelligence and quantum chemistry to design sunlight-activated materials that break down pollutants in water. The award comes with a $250,000 grant , and Xatoms was chosen from more than 2,000 applications.

Most of the AI conversation at Climate Week focused on what AI takes from the planet: power, land and, increasingly, water. Xatoms offers a positive counterpoint, a case study in AI giving back.

A personal mission, not a market opportunity

Most founders find a market. Virgovicova found a problem the hard way. She grew up in a village of about 800 people in Slovakia , surrounded by farms that used heavy amounts of pesticides. “I got sick when I was 14 years old,” she told me. “I was diagnosed with ovarian cancer because of the water I drank.”

After her diagnosis, she persuaded her mother to go backpacking across Asia. On trains in India, she heard from women facing the same thing. “I learned that there is a girl in Slovakia who got sick. There is a girl in India who’s getting infections. There is a girl in Africa who has to spend long hours every single day searching for clean water,” she said. “So, we need to find a solution, and it is affecting mainly women across the globe.”

Globally, women and girls spend 250 million hours a day collecting water, more than three times the time men and boys spend. “While boys go to school, the girls are responsible for bringing a bucket of water home, and they start missing school very early on,” Virgovicova explained. “It’s an educational, economic and health problem.”

And it’s growing. “We have 2 billion people that don’t have access to clean drinking water, and this number is actually growing because of f

summary.tldr:
Diana Virgovicova, founder and CEO of Toronto-based Xatoms, won the 2026 Global Citizen Prize: Cisco Youth Leadership Award at Climate Week in New York, receiving a $250,000 grant selected from over 2,000 applications. Xatoms utilizes artificial intelligence and quantum chemistry to computationally design sunlight-activated photocatalytic materials that break down complex industrial water contaminants, such as pesticides, pharmaceuticals, forever chemicals, and heavy metals, bypassing traditional water treatment limits that focus primarily on bacteria like E. coli.

While traditional materials discovery takes up to a decade in physical laboratories, Xatoms leverages an AI-driven computational pipeline to design and evaluate molecules in 30 days. The core output is a photocatalytic powder that splits water into hydroxyl (OH) radicals under visible sunlight or LEDs—eliminating the need for expensive ultraviolet reactors—and is not consumed during the process, allowing small amounts to treat hundreds of gallons. Beyond addressing global drinking water deficits affecting 2 billion people, Xatoms is targeting data center cooling water reuse to counteract the immense water consumption footprints of modern AI buildouts, alongside ongoing deployments in Canadian Indigenous communities, Kenya, South Africa, Japan, and Azerbaijan.

The startup currently manages 88 different material options customized to specific water samples and contaminant profiles, with six major commercial projects forthcoming. Virgovicova noted that climate venture capital funding allocates roughly only 3% to water initiatives despite its foundational role across agriculture, industry, and AI infrastructure.
takeaways: **Award and Grant:** Diana Virgovicova won the 2026 Global Citizen Prize: Cisco Youth Leadership Award, securing a $250,000 grant out of more than 2,000 applicants.
**Technology Pipeline:** Xatoms combines quantum chemistry and AI to reduce materials discovery timelines from a decade down to 30 days without initial physical laboratory synthesis.

**Catalytic Mechanism:** The engineered photocatalytic powder uses visible light or LEDs rather than ultraviolet light to split water into OH radicals that destroy complex industrial pollutants like pharmaceuticals and heavy metals.
**Data Center Application:** Xatoms is positioning its catalytic treatment to enable water reuse inside data center cooling systems to mitigate the infrastructure's environmental footprint.

**Global Footprint:** The company maintains a portfolio of 88 material options customized for specific regional water samples, with active projects in Canada, Kenya, South Africa, Japan, and Azerbaijan.

title: Zyphra AI Introduces Zyphra Hierarchical Attention (ZHA): A Path to True Subquadratic Attention
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: Zyphra has released Zyphra Hierarchical Attention (ZHA) , a sparse attention method built around a tree-structured indexer. ZHA targets a known gap in sparse attention: the indexer that picks tokens still scans the whole context. Zyphra’s technical paper shows ZHA can be distilled into frozen pretrained models with about 4B tokens. On Qwen3.6-35B-A3B it stays close to dense attention on reasoning, agentic coding and 256K retrieval benchmarks. TL;DR Size: It is a method that adds 81,920 trainable parameters to Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (about 0.00024%). Tested up to 256K context. Runs on: Retrofits frozen pretrained models after a 4B-token KL warmup at 32K context. Speedups come from a modeled H100 BF16 roofline. No optimized kernels released. An FP4 router variant was also tested. Performance: Within a few points of dense attention on 7 reasoning, coding and retrieval benchmarks. Best: LongBench v2 hits 63.4% (deep tree) vs 58.0% dense, using about 1.1% of keys. Worst: On NoPE-based Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B, deep-tree RULER-13 drops 25.3 points below dense. What is Zyphra Hierarchical Attention (ZHA)? ZHA is a sparse attention method from Zyphra that finds relevant keys by searching a tree. It keeps the full KV cache. The tree only decides which cached keys each query reads. Fixed-state methods like SSMs and sliding windows saturate at long contexts. Fine-grained sparse methods like DeepSeek Sparse Attention score every past token with an indexer. The final attention is sparse, but the indexer still grows with the full context. Near 1M tokens, cited work shows indexing takes 60 to 90% of layer time. ZHA makes the search itself sparse. How does ZHA’s tree indexer work? Building the tree ZHA splits keys into contiguous chunks and compresses each chunk into a summary key. Summaries are grouped and compressed again, level by level. With chunk size 4, 6 levels cover 4,096 tokens per top node. Summaries come from a small set of learned reference queries . Each reference query gives a tangent-plane estimate of a chunk’s log attention mass. The max over these planes approximates how much attention any future query would give the chunk. How does top-p routing pick tokens? At decode time, a query scores the top-level nodes. It keeps the smallest set holding a fraction p of estimated attention mass. It then expands only those children, repeating until it reaches raw KV ent

ZHA targets a known gap in sparse attention: the indexer that picks tokens still scans the whole context. Zyphra’s technical paper shows ZHA can be distilled into frozen pretrained models with about 4B tokens.

On Qwen3.6-35B-A3B it stays close to dense attention on reasoning, agentic coding and 256K retrieval benchmarks. TL;DR Size: It is a method that adds 81,920 trainable parameters to Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (about 0.00024%). Tested up to 256K context.

title: The Letter Company Releases Letterpress-1: A Coding Agent Built for Growth Engineering
author: Michal Sutter
contentSnippet: The Letter Company has released the beta of Letterpress-1 , a coding agent, harness and IDE for growth engineering. The Letterpress-1 coding agent reads a website and its market, then decides what should exist. It builds the change in a sandbox and opens a pull request with a live preview. TL;DR Size: Letter team says it combines frontier models with fine-tuned small models; names and sizes are not disclosed. Runs on: Letter’s hosted platform against your git repository. No local GPU needed. Setup takes under 5 minutes, per Letter. Performance: No public benchmark. Letter shows 1 self-reported, side-by-side page build against Codex. Best: 760 tools exposed through 1 registry over MCP, REST and CLI. Worst: No measurable eval; entry plan is $100/month with overage at 5x the list rate. What is Letterpress-1? Letterpress-1 is a growth engineering agent from The Letter Company. It turns site and market signals into pull requests. The letter company team argues that websites, unlike apps, react to outside forces. These include agent behavior, Google rankings, human visits and competitor activity . General coding agents were built to scale codebases, not to act on those signals. The agent is aimed at teams that host their marketing site in git. It is proactive: it suggests the next thing to build. Examples include de-anonymization, landing pages, warmed emails, blog automation and agent telemetry. How does Letterpress-1 work? Letterpress-1 runs in 3 modes : Build: create a page or feature from a prompt, with brand copy and visuals kept consistent. Plan: pick a goal and get a build plan of growth actions. Fix: find site issues and dispatch pull requests to fix them. Every change follows the same loop. The agent reads the site, plans and builds in a sandbox. It reviews its own change, then opens a pull request. Each change returns a preview link of your own site . Nothing lands until you choose a preview, a pull request, or a merge after checks pass. Letter team lists 6 surfaces. These are the web platform, a Slack app, the letterpress CLI and a website portal. A standalone app and your own agent round out the list. The in-site IDE works on a live page. Press ⌘L, edit text where you see it, and a pull request follows. Showcase examples also cover A/B tests from live edits. For developers, agents.md documents an MCP server at app.letterstory.com/api/mcp with OAuth. Th

title: llm 0.37
author: Simon Willison AI
contentSnippet: Release: llm 0.37 There's a lot of stuff in this new release of my LLM CLI tool and Python library, representing around two months of accumulated features and fixes. I added gpt-6.1-sol and gpt-6.1-terra , plus a new llm openai endpoint add command to make it easier to configure additional models that use OpenAI-compatible endpoints. I switched the default model (if you have not set your own default) to gpt-6-luna - half the price of the previous default, gpt-5.6-luna . LLM's support for embeddings now accepts that different binary content may have different content-type - necessary for models like Gemini Embedding 2 , which can embed text, audio, images, and video. A lot of open source maintainers complain about a flood of AI-assisted PRs. LLM is my project that has been most affected by this and, to be honest, I'm not finding it to be a problem. That's mainly because I have Opus 5.5 or GPT-6 Astra help me with triage to spot the most useful fixes! This release includes fixes from 12 authors - almost all AI-assisted - and the burden of reviewing them wasn't nearly as great as I expected. I really see them as bug reports with attached examples - sometimes I land them, sometimes I implement my own fix. title: Rack-scale AI: How Dell and AMD are building infrastructure
author: Mark Albertson
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 18:33 EST / NOVEMBER 02 2026

Rack-scale AI: How Dell and AMD are building infrastructure

Dell Technologies Inc. and its partner Advanced Micro Devices Inc. face similar competitive pressures. Both tech powerhouses operate in a business climate where success is now measured across central processing units, graphics processing units, rack-scale systems, memory capacity, network bandwidth and tokens per dollar.

The pressure to compete across those measures underscores what theCUBE Research has termed “Engineering Velocity.” Since the Dell Technologies World event in May, AMD and Dell have not slowed their pace of collaborations and announcements.

AMD and Dell are working to build enterprise AI infrastructure that can keep pace with changing workloads and customer requirements.

“In AI infrastructure, the winner may not be the company with the best benchmark on keynote day,” said theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante . “It will more likely be the company whose engineering system learns, validates and improves the entire platform faster than anyone else.”

This feature is part of SiliconANGLE Media’s exploration of the architectural shifts powering continuous, production-grade AI. Be sure to check out theCUBE’s “Dell AI Data Platform Event: From Ambition to AI at Scale” and its past coverage of this year’s Dell Technologies World . (* Disclosure below.)

Rack-scale consolidation

A cornerstone of the Dell and AMD relationship is the server giant’s PowerEdge portfolio. Dell expanded its PowerEdge server line in May and has followed that up with additional details surrounding the integration of AMD processors.

The two companies have pursued a strategy designed to facilitate server consolidation as agentic AI drives a surge in demand for general-purpose compute. Agents rely heavily on CPUs, yet data centers don’t have a lot of extra room to add servers in rooms already stacked with GPUs.

Systems powered by AMD processors will deliver 70% gen-over-gen performance gains and can fold 13 servers from Dell’s 14th PowerEdge generation into one, according to Pradyumna Narendra , product planner and senior consultant at Dell.

“For every 10 to 13 servers you replace, you get so much of that productivity gain back because now you can do that with one server,” he told theCUBE . “When you expand that across data centers, that’s like an accelerating effect that you get

summary.tldr:
Dell Technologies and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) are expanding their hardware and infrastructure collaboration to address enterprise AI workloads, focusing on rack-scale systems, server consolidation, and modular deployments. According to Dell representatives, systems powered by newer AMD processors deliver 70% generation-over-generation performance gains, allowing enterprises to consolidate up to 13 servers from older 14th-generation PowerEdge lines into a single modern unit. This density helps mitigate space and cooling constraints in existing data center footprints as agentic AI and high-throughput inference workloads scale.

The partnership centers on the Dell AI Platform with AMD, which integrates AMD Instinct accelerators and EPYC processors with Dell PowerEdge servers, PowerSwitch networking, and PowerScale storage. The companies have incorporated the AMD ROCm software stack to support local model training, fine-tuning, and serving. Notably, Dell added support for AMD Instinct MI350P PCI Express GPUs in its PowerEdge XE7745 and R7725 servers starting in July, featuring 144 gigabytes of HBM3E memory to optimize time-to-first-token latency for inference. To address enterprise hesitancy toward liquid cooling, the PCIe-based GPUs support air-cooled deployments.

Beyond standard enterprise servers, the collaboration spans joint high-performance computing and telecom initiatives. Dell and AMD partnered with the University of Cambridge to establish a Sovereign AI Innovation Lab utilizing Zenith AI supercomputers powered by fifth-generation EPYC processors and MI355X GPUs. Additionally, they teamed up with AT&T to provide hardware infrastructure—such as Dell's PowerEdge XE9785 servers configured with eight MI355X GPUs—for training and inference workloads using OTel 2.0 models developed through the Open Telco AI initiative.
takeaways: **Server Consolidation Metrics:** AMD-powered Dell systems deliver 70% gen-over-gen performance gains, enabling enterprises to replace 13 servers from the 14th PowerEdge generation with a single server.
**GPU Memory Specifications:** The AMD Instinct MI350P PCIe GPU features 144 gigabytes of HBM3E memory, designed to reduce time-to-first-token latency for inference workloads.

**Air-Cooled Enterprise Integration:** Dell added support for AMD's air-cooled PCIe-based Instinct GPUs in PowerEdge XE7745 and R7725 servers to accommodate enterprises not yet prepared to adopt direct liquid cooling.

**Academic and Telecom Deployments:** The collaboration includes powering the University of Cambridge's Sovereign AI Innovation Lab (Zenith AI supercomputer) and AT&T's OTel 2.0 model training using Dell PowerEdge XE9785 servers with eight MI355X GPUs.

title: Anthropic’s quarterly revenue jumps to $17B, losses grow ahead of IPO
author: Maria Deutscher
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 18:19 EST / NOVEMBER 02 2026

Anthropic’s quarterly revenue jumps to $17B, losses grow ahead of IPO

Anthropic PBC today published an updated version of the S-1 filing for its upcoming public offering.

The original document, which the company released last Monday, didn’t contain its third-quarter financial results. The new version reveals that Anthropic generated $17 billion in revenue during the three months ended Sept. 30. That’s more than 11 times more than what it made a year earlier, but represents a deacceleration in quarter-over-quarter growth. Anthropic’s top line grew 47% on a quarterly basis, down from 144% three months earlier.

The artificial intelligence provider faces multipronged competition from open-source models, OpenAI Group PBC and tech giants such as Google LLC. The Alphabet Inc.’s newest model, Gemini 4 Carbon, outperforms Claude Opus 5.5 across multiple benchmarks.

Anthropic is investing heavily in training infrastructure to stay ahead of the competition. The company took a $5 billion charge in the third quarter because demand for computing hardware was higher than expected, which required it to purchase hardware at a premium. Hardware bought on short notice is more expensive than Anthropic’s usual capacity commitments, which it books 12 to 18 months before they’re needed.

The AI provider also took a $2 billion charge in connection with its non-cash employee donation matching program. That left Anthropic with a $536 million operating loss at the end of the third quarter. Three months earlier, it posted $974 million in operating income. Anthropic’s adjusted operating income, which excludes stock-based compensation and charitable contributions, jumped by $300 million on a quarterly basis to $2.5 billion.

The company had $895.4 billion in outstanding infrastructure commitments as of Sept 30. Leases signed with Google LLC and Broadcom Inc. accounted for nearly a third of that sum. In April, the two companies agreed to supply Anthropic with several gigawatts of computing power powered by the search giant’s TPU chips, which Broadcom helped design. The AI provider also has computing deals with Amazon.com Inc., Oracle Corp. and SpaceX Technologies Corp. that are each worth more than $100 billion.

Anthropic plans to not only rent more computing capacity but also build its own data centers. The company’s purchase commitments jumped

summary.tldr:
Anthropic PBC has published an updated S-1 filing for its upcoming public offering, revealing third-quarter revenue of $17 billion for the period ended September 30, 2026. This represents an 11-fold year-over-year increase, though quarterly growth decelerated to 47% down from 144% in the previous quarter. The company faces stiff competition from Google LLC, whose Gemini 4 Carbon model outperforms Claude Opus 5.5 across multiple benchmarks.

To secure computational resources, Anthropic booked massive infrastructure commitments totaling $895.4 billion as of September 30, with future purchase commitments surging to approximately $314 billion. The third quarter included a $5 billion charge for premium hardware acquired on short notice due to higher-than-expected demand, alongside a $2 billion charge for a non-cash employee donation matching program. These expenses resulted in a $536 million operating loss for the quarter, contrasting with $974 million in operating income three months prior, though adjusted operating income rose by $300 million to $2.5 billion. Major infrastructure agreements include gigawatt-scale TPU capacity leases with Google and Broadcom Inc., plus multi-hundred-billion-dollar deals with Amazon.com Inc., Oracle Corp., and SpaceX Technologies Corp.

Ahead of its IPO, Anthropic is seeking a valuation between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion, with fundraising aspirations matching or exceeding SpaceX's $86.2 billion listing earlier in the year. The updated S-1 filing also notes that Anthropic is considering mandatory human review for specific automated research tasks as its models approach capabilities that could dramatically accelerate internal AI development.
takeaways: **Third-Quarter Revenue:** Anthropic generated $17 billion in revenue for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, marking an 11x year-over-year increase but a quarterly growth deceleration to 47% from 144% the prior quarter.

**Operating Losses and Financial Charges:** The company posted a $536 million operating loss in Q3 due to a $5 billion charge for premium short-notice hardware purchases and a $2 billion charge for a non-cash employee donation matching program, while adjusted operating income reached $2.5 billion.

**Infrastructure Commitments:** Outstanding infrastructure commitments reached $895.4 billion by September 30, 2026, with individual computing deals with Amazon, Oracle, and SpaceX each valued at over $100 billion, alongside leases with Google and Broadcom.
**IPO Targets and Valuation:** Anthropic is targeting an IPO valuation between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion, aiming to surpass the $86.2 billion raised by SpaceX earlier in the year.

title: Trajectory raises $45M to make AI model training accessible to nontechnical experts
author: Marina Temkin
contentSnippet:
Whether developed by OpenAI or Anthropic or built on open source alternatives, current AI models share a critical limitation: They don’t learn from their mistakes without further training.

Businesses adapting these models for specialized fields, such as law and finance, typically get around this by fine-tuning general models. However, that often requires hiring internal research teams or relying on expensive consultants, commonly known as forward-deployed engineers (FDEs).

Trajectory , a startup founded about a year ago by three Stanford classmates with experience at Google DeepMind and Apple, wants to automate that process, allowing AI models to learn from feedback and continuously improve at specialized tasks.

The 18-person company just announced that it raised $45 million in a Series A round at a $300 million valuation, led by Sequoia, with participation from Nvidia, Bessemer Venture Partners, and Bain Capital Ventures.

Trajectory co-founder Ronak Malde compared foundational models to a very smart PhD student who’s always starting a new job. “But what the economy values is someone who worked on the job for 30 years,” he told TechCrunch.

The startup aims to solve this problem through an approach known as continual learning. Businesses using Trajectory can start with an open source AI model and connect the platform to their applications, allowing it to collect feedback on how the model performs. Trajectory then uses that information to retrain the model, helping it improve at specialized tasks over time.

With Trajectory, lawyers, doctors, and other specialists can improve the models near automatically themselves, Malde said. That capability could make deploying specialized AI faster and cheaper.

Companies like Harvey and Rogo are already using Trajectory’s platform to post-train open source models, helping them perform more like experienced lawyers or financial analysts by learning from previous tasks, such as reviewing a particular type of legal contract or valuing a company using a specific methodology. Trajectory’s other customers include Decagon, Mercor, and Nvidia. The startup is now making its post-training platform publicly available.

The people using Trajectory decide “what good looks like for their organization and can turn that into improvements for their model,” Malde said.

Trajectory’s approach to continual learning shares some similari

summary.tldr:
Trajectory, an 18-person startup founded by Stanford alumni with backgrounds at Google DeepMind and Apple, has raised $45 million in a Series A funding round at a $300 million valuation. Led by Sequoia, the round also included participation from Nvidia, Bessemer Venture Partners, and Bain Capital Ventures. The company is publicly launching a post-training platform designed to automate AI model fine-tuning and continual learning for nontechnical enterprise users.

Traditional AI deployment requires businesses to hire internal research teams or expensive forward-deployed engineers (FDEs) to adapt foundation models for specialized domains like law and finance. Trajectory allows enterprises to connect open-source models to its platform, collect performance feedback from user applications, and automatically retrain models to improve over time. Co-founder Ronak Malde contrasts current foundational models with fresh PhD graduates, positioning Trajectory's continual learning approach as a way to simulate decades of on-the-job experience. Early enterprise customers include Harvey, Rogo, Decagon, Mercor, and Nvidia.

While sharing operational similarities with recursive self-improvement, co-founder Michael Elabd emphasizes that keeping humans in the loop makes Trajectory's training loop safer. The startup competes with Thinking Machines Lab (creators of Tinker, founded by former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati), Applied Compute, and Prime Intellect. Trajectory's founding team includes Ronak Malde (formerly of Google DeepMind and Windsurf), Michael Elabd (Google DeepMind), and Arjun Karanam (Apple generative models), alongside hires recruited from OpenAI, Stripe, and Netflix.
takeaways: **Funding & Valuation:** Trajectory raised a $45 million Series A at a $300 million valuation led by Sequoia, with participation from Nvidia, Bessemer Venture Partners, and Bain Capital Ventures.

**Founding Team:** The 18-person startup was founded one year ago by Stanford alumni Ronak Malde (ex-Google DeepMind/Windsurf), Michael Elabd (ex-Google DeepMind), and Arjun Karanam (ex-Apple generative foundation models).
**Customer Base:** Early adopters using Trajectory to post-train open-source models include Harvey, Rogo, Decagon, Mercor, and Nvidia.

**Competitive Landscape:** Trajectory competes directly with Thinking Machines Lab (maker of Tinker, founded by former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati), Applied Compute (valued at $3.25 billion), and Prime Intellect.

title: 42AI launches with $62.5M to predict how traders act when markets turn volatile
author: Duncan Riley
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 17:47 EST / NOVEMBER 02 2026

42AI launches with $62.5M to predict how traders act when markets turn volatile

Israeli artificial intelligence startup 42AI launched today with $62.5 million in funding to build what it calls a behavioral world model.

Its first customers are brokerages that want to know how individual traders will act when markets turn volatile. 42AI offers software that estimates the odds of each choice a person might make in a given situation. “Behavior is not deterministic; it’s constantly probabilistic,” co-founder and Chief Executive Amit Gal-Or told TechCrunch .

The company turns what it knows about a person into mathematical representations of personality traits, and a transformer-based world model works out the probabilities from there. A separate language model writes up which traits and context drove each prediction.

42AI says a brokerage can see what each client is likely to trade over the next 24 hours, including the instrument, the direction and the volume. If clients look set to pile into the same trade, a risk desk can hedge before the exposure lands on its book. Know-your-customer checks done at onboarding are one source of input, and the model also weighs how often a client calls and the sentiment in their voice.

Ten large brokerages are working with 42AI, which charges either a flat fee or a percentage of the value it helps generate. Revenue has reached seven figures, Gal-Or said, without giving a precise number.

By the company’s account, one brokerage gained about $30 million in additional value through dynamic hedging. The company also claims 98% accuracy on trades. That figure tracks whether trading flows land inside a predicted range, according to Gal-Or, and does not measure whether every individual trade was predicted correctly.

Three years of research went into the model. Thousands of people took psychological assessments in the first study, and by the time the team moved on to government and biobank datasets, the sample had passed 2 million. Customer data now spans about 30 million people.

Chief Technology Officer Ehud Ezra and three co-authors described one piece of the work in a paper posted in February . Their Large Behavioral Model adapts an 8 billion-parameter version of Meta Platforms Inc.’s Llama 3.1 to predict a person’s strategic choices from a detailed psychometric profile.

summary.tldr:
Israeli artificial intelligence startup 42AI has launched out of stealth with $62.5 million in seed funding from founders and Infinity Group to build what it terms a "behavioral world model." Co-founded and led by CEO Amit Gal-Or alongside CTO Ehud Ezra—with advisory support from 2011 Nobel Prize in Chemistry laureate Dan Shechtman—the company targets brokerages seeking to predict individual trader behavior during market volatility. The software estimates probabilistic outcomes for user decisions using mathematical personality representations processed by a transformer-based world model, paired with a language model that generates textual rationales for each prediction.

The underlying Large Behavioral Model adapts an 8 billion-parameter version of Meta Platforms Inc.’s Llama 3.1 to forecast strategic human choices from psychometric profiles. Inputs include onboarding know-your-customer data, call frequency metrics, and vocal sentiment. The system claims 98% accuracy, defined specifically as trading flows landing within a predicted range rather than exact individual trade hits. Ten large brokerages currently utilize the platform under flat-fee or value-percentage pricing models, generating seven-figure revenues, with one client reportedly capturing approximately $30 million in additional value via dynamic hedging.

Following three years of research and training datasets scaling from thousands of psychological assessment participants to government and biobank datasets covering over 2 million people—and current customer data spanning roughly 30 million individuals—42AI plans to expand into gaming, fraud prevention, cybersecurity, and eventual robotics and AI agent applications. While executives acknowledge privacy safeguards via anonymized identifiers, internal ethics committees, and regulatory monitoring, the founders note a natural performance ceiling exists when subjects act on unaccounted external influences, such as unrecorded colleague advice.
takeaways: **Funding and Leadership:** 42AI launched with $62.5 million in seed funding accumulated over three years from its founders and Infinity Group, led by CEO Amit Gal-Or, Chairman Amir Gal-Or, and CTO Ehud Ezra, with Nobel laureate Dan Shechtman serving as an adviser.

**Model Architecture:** The startup's Large Behavioral Model fine-tunes an 8 billion-parameter version of Meta's Llama 3.1, translating personal psychometric traits and behavioral inputs (like call frequency and voice sentiment) into probabilistic choices via a transformer-based world model and a separate language model.

**Performance and Scale:** The system processes data spanning approximately 30 million people across 10 large brokerages, claiming a 98% accuracy rate defined by trading flows falling inside predicted ranges, contributing to seven-figure revenue and one reported case of $30 million in dynamic hedging value.

**Future Roadmaps:** 42AI is actively exploring expansion into gaming, fraud prevention, and cybersecurity, with a long-term goal of enabling robots and AI agents to model and understand human behavior.

title: Anthropic warns that it’s very close to RSI capability, aka self-building AI
author: Julie Bort
contentSnippet:
While much attention has focused on the updated financials Anthropic revealed in its revised S-1A on Monday, (revenue is soaring, but so are expenses), the AI lab dropped another little bombshell in the fine print.

The filing seems to warn that the company is on the cusp of creating a model capable of recursive self-improvement (RSI).

RSI is the point at which AI grows so good at training itself that it spawns a dramatic acceleration of AI capabilities. To the AI doomers, RSI represents the cataclysm from which there is no return, in which AI builds itself into something powerful enough that it slips beyond human control and may be indifferent to the damage it causes while achieving its goals.

To AI enthusiasts, RSI, or some version of AI reliably using itself to improve, represents the technology’s promise, where it becomes a tool of unimaginable productivity, scientific discovery, and more.

Anthropic seems to believe that RSI is both a promise and a peril. It says in the S-1 that it uses AI in its R&D, but it cautions: “Using AI to help build more capable AI could also pose a considerable safety risk, particularly if it sharply accelerates the pace of progress. This is one of the areas covered by our Responsible Scaling Policy, which sets out our plans to monitor and mitigate the risks as we approach what has been termed ‘recursive self-improvement.’”

When the term RSI became popular earlier this year , many believed it was a buzzword or, at best, a goal too hard to achieve, define, or prove.

But on Monday, Anthropic added new statements to its Risk Factors section, saying 1) it has already used AI to develop new models whose leaps in capability it didn’t recognize at the time, and 2) it may soon meet its own internal definition of RSI (bold emphasis ours, below):

In addition, our increasing use of AI systems to accelerate our own research and development may cause the capabilities of our models to advance more rapidly than our ability to develop, validate, and implement corresponding safety, alignment, and security measures. As a result, we have in the past not identified , and may in the future not identify, a significant acceleration in our rate of development until after it has occurred.

For example, our internal estimates and our expectations regarding future models, rather than our current models, indicate that we may imminently meet our Resp

summary.tldr:
Anthropic disclosed in a revised S-1A filing that it is nearing the threshold of recursive self-improvement (RSI), a milestone where AI systems are used to build more capable AI, potentially accelerating progress beyond human safety and alignment capabilities. The company noted that internal estimates indicate future models may imminently meet its Responsible Scaling Policy definition for "dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI," though it confirmed that none of its current models have crossed this threshold.

The filing highlights that Anthropic has previously failed to immediately identify significant capability accelerations resulting from AI-driven research and development. Despite nearing these technical limits, the lab stated it does not anticipate safely deploying Claude to fully autonomously design and build successive frontier models without meaningful human supervision, and is considering updates to keep humans in control of frontier development.
takeaways: **S-1A Filing Disclosures:** Anthropic added explicit warnings to the Risk Factors section of its revised S-1A regarding the use of AI systems to accelerate internal research and development.

**Responsible Scaling Policy:** Internal estimates suggest future models may imminently meet Anthropic's policy threshold for "dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI," though current models have not crossed it.
**Unidentified Acceleration:** Anthropic admitted it has previously failed to identify significant acceleration in its rate of development until after the capability leaps had already occurred.
**Human Supervision Commitment:** The lab stated it does not plan to use Claude for fully autonomous design and building of successive frontier models without meaningful human supervision.

title: Grok Bot users hit with weekly limits early, Elon Musk explains what happened
author: Joey Klender
contentSnippet: Elon Musk said weeks ago during SpaceX’s third-quarter earnings call that the company’s Grok Bot, its autonomous AI Agent platform, was showing “the fastest growth of a product” that he’d ever seen in his life. Now, SpaceXSI is scaling back Grok Bot users’ weekly limits, much to the surprise of those who have relied on it to take away monotonous tasks in their lives. Elon Musk’s terse November 1 reply on X captured a sharp tension in the early days of agentic AI. Responding to a user who asked for a Grok Bot usage reset after hitting 100 percent with four days still left on the weekly cycle, Musk wrote: “The cost of serving Grok Bot was unsustainably high relative to revenue.” @DogecoinNorway The cost of serving Grok Bot was unsustainably high relative to revenue — Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 1, 2026 The post arrived amid a wave of similar complaints from paying subscribers whose meters had jumped unexpectedly toward or to the limit, sometimes overnight and with little corresponding activity. It also stood in clear contrast to statements Musk had made only days and weeks earlier. On the SpaceX third-quarter earnings call in mid-to-late October, Musk had described Grok Bot in almost the opposite terms . He called it “the fastest growth of a product that I’ve ever seen in my life” and said he had “never seen anything grow this fast.” Company figures put paid weekly users at roughly 800,000 earlier in the month, more than doubling over the prior period. Daily active users had climbed from under 100,000 in early September to over 600,000 by late October. Musk emphasized that the product has no free tier and that users appear to be getting real value beyond what they pay. In other remarks , he noted that usage per user was rising rather than declining, the opposite of the usual decay pattern for new software. Grok Bot, launched around August, functions as an always-available agent with its own persistent cloud computer; it can schedule, research, shop, browse, and execute multi-step workflows even after the user steps away. Access is bundled into X subscription tiers (roughly $30, $100, and $200 per month) and certain Cursor plans, drawing from shared weekly usage pools whose exact sizes have not been publicly detailed. The economics of that model are what Musk’s November 1 post put in the spotlight. Agentic systems burn far more compute than ordinary chatbot

title: Deep Principle Releases Hydrogen-1.0: A 753B Open-Weight Model for Scientific Discovery
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: Deep Principle has released Hydrogen-1.0 , an open-weight scientific model for chemistry, materials science and life sciences. It is built by post-training Z.ai’s GLM-5.3 on domain data, laboratory records and agent discovery trajectories. For developers, it offers open weights that report a FrontierScience-Research win over GPT-6-Astra. The weights ship under the MIT License. TL;DR Size: 753B parameters (MoE, ~40B active per the GLM-5.3 base), 1M-token context, 128K max output. Runs on: 8 GPUs with SGLang (tested); NVFP4 for NVIDIA B200/B300, MXFP4 for AMD MI350X/MI355X. Performance: Beats GPT-6-Astra on FrontierScience-Research; roughly matches Kimi-K3 on GPQA-Diamond. Best: 38.3% on FrontierScience-Research vs 33.3% for GPT-6-Astra (self-reported). Worst: Trails GPT-6-Astra (max thinking) by 3.33 points on NMR structure elucidation. What is Hydrogen-1.0? Hydrogen-1.0 is a scientific research assistant model from Deep Principle, a Hangzhou-based AI-for-materials company. The model card describes it as a GLM-5.3 derivative for scientific problem solving. It targets question framing, experiment planning, results analysis and open-ended discovery. Deep Principle team states that proprietary models produced recent AI science results, but their discovery capabilities are not open. Hydrogen-1.0 is its attempt at a reproducible, inspectable alternative. How was Hydrogen-1.0 trained? The pipeline combines supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with reinforcement learning (RL). Data comes from 4 sources: Domain knowledge: chemistry, materials science and life sciences data. Research scenarios: task-specific feedback from Deep Principle scientists. Laboratory records: full-cycle electronic lab notebook records captured through Mira . Discovery trajectories: sequences of choices and feedback, including failed attempts. Infrastructure builds on Megatron and SGLang across NVIDIA CUDA and AMD ROCm. The team keeps dynamic sparse attention causal across context-parallel shards. Muon optimizer state is moved between CPU, GPU and disk per backend. RL uses resumable rollouts, and each token keeps its original behavior log-probability for importance correction. A layout adapter converts training checkpoints into BF16 and 128×128 blockwise FP8 inference weights. Full datasets and recipes are not released. How does Hydrogen-1.0 perform on benchmarks? title: Prepare web content for Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with Crawl4AI
author: Daxeshkumar Patel
contentSnippet: When you build Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) applications, answer quality depends on the data that you ingest. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases is the fully managed RAG capability of Amazon Bedrock. With Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base , you connect your data sources, and Amazon Bedrock manages ingestion, storage, indexing, and retrieval for you. You don’t provision or scale a vector store, and embedding and reranking use service-managed models by default. For web content, start with the Amazon Bedrock Web Crawler data source connector for managed knowledge bases. You give it the seed URLs or sitemaps that you’re authorized to crawl, and it crawls within the scope and rate limits that you set. Scheduled syncs keep your knowledge base current as pages change, and the connector can wait for content that loads with JavaScript. There’s no crawler for you to build, host, or operate, so this connector is the starting point for most public website content. Some sources need more control over what reaches the knowledge base. You might want to index only the main content region of each page, remove navigation and other boilerplate, or attach your own metadata attributes to every document. For that class of source material, you can extend the reach of your knowledge base with a preparation step built with Crawl4AI , an open source Python crawler. The step writes Markdown and a metadata sidecar for each page to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), and the knowledge base ingests both through its Amazon S3 data source. In this post, we show you how to choose the appropriate web ingestion path and implement custom preparation for content that needs additional processing. You then start ingestion into a managed knowledge base and validate retrieval quality. The companion aws-samples repository provides the complete workflow as a sample implementation. This is batch ingestion of known web properties, not real-time web access at inference time such as Web Grounding with Amazon Nova. Solution overview Start with the Amazon Bedrock Web Crawler when it can reach and index the pages you need. It respects robots.txt , and after the first full crawl, each sync captures only added, updated, and deleted content. With Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base , you connect your data sources, and Amazon Bedrock manages ingestion, storage, indexing, and retrieval for you.

You don’t provision or scale a vector store, and embedding and reranking use service-managed models by default. For web content, start with the Amazon Bedrock Web Crawler data source connector for managed knowledge bases. You give it the seed URLs or sitemaps that you’re authorized to crawl, and it crawls within the scope and rate limits that you set.

title: Build efficient agents with knowledge distillation on Amazon SageMaker AI
author: Giuseppe Zappia
contentSnippet: You built a shopping assistant on a frontier model, and it works. A shopper asks for “a black waist bag under twenty dollars from a shop with at least 4.5 stars,” and the agent searches the catalog, inspects candidates, checks the constraints, and commits to a recommendation. But what does that interaction actually cost? An agentic assistant is not one model call, it is a loop: search, read results, refine, verify, decide. A single completed task can be multiple calls to that frontier model, and you pay for every one, on every shopper. At production scale, that per-task cost compounds, erodes the project’s ROI, and stops the project from shipping. One way to make an agentic application more efficient is to use a smaller model, which is faster to respond and more cost-effective to host. The catch is quality: a smaller model usually falls short on the task, which is why the larger one was chosen in the first place. Knowledge distillation closes that gap by transferring the behavior of the larger “teacher” model into a smaller “student”, training the student to reproduce the teacher’s outputs, so it keeps much of the quality at the smaller model’s speed and cost. In this post you will learn how to use knowledge distillation, and specifically sequence-level knowledge distillation (SeqKD), to fine-tune a shopping agent on Amazon SageMaker AI . We cover how to generate high-quality multi-step trajectories with a frontier teacher and keep the ones that solve the task, how to encode them for supervised fine-tuning, how to run the training on serverless infrastructure, and how to evaluate the student against a held-out benchmark. Figure 1: One agentic task is a loop, not a single call: the agent searches, reads results, refines, verifies, and decides, and each step is a separate billed call to the frontier model. A single completed task can be multiple calls, on every shopper What is sequence-level knowledge distillation (SeqKD)? The simplest applicable form of distillation is sequence-level knowledge distillation (SeqKD). It uses a teacher model to generate high-quality responses, then trains a student model on those responses with supervised fine-tuning (SFT). SeqKD needs only the teacher’s text , with no access to teacher logits and no reinforcement-learning infrastructure, so it works even with a closed or API-only teacher. Compared to other approaches such as lo

summary.tldr:
Amazon Web Services has released a technical guide on using sequence-level knowledge distillation (SeqKD) to optimize agentic AI applications hosted on Amazon SageMaker AI. The methodology addresses the high operational costs associated with multi-step agentic loops—where models perform iterative tasks like searching, reading, refining, and verifying—by transferring the behavioral capabilities of a large 'teacher' frontier model to a smaller, more cost-effective 'student' model.

SeqKD functions by using the teacher model to generate high-quality, multi-step task trajectories, which are then used as training data for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of the student model. This approach is specifically designed for API-only or closed-source teacher models, as it requires only the output text rather than access to internal logits or complex reinforcement learning infrastructure. The workflow detailed by AWS covers the generation of successful task trajectories, data encoding for SFT, execution on serverless infrastructure, and benchmarking the student model against held-out datasets to ensure performance parity.
takeaways: **Methodology:** SeqKD utilizes supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on teacher-generated text outputs to train smaller student models without requiring access to teacher model logits.
**Operational Efficiency:** The approach targets the reduction of per-task costs in agentic loops, where multiple model calls are typically required for a single user request.
**Infrastructure:** The training process is designed to run on Amazon SageMaker AI, utilizing serverless infrastructure for the fine-tuning phase.
**Scope:** The technique is specifically applicable to closed or API-only frontier models where internal model weights or probability distributions are inaccessible.

title: Agentic engineering intelligence with Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
author: Aishwarya Gavili
contentSnippet: When a qualified aerospace component goes obsolete or hits a long lead time, an engineer spends days cross-referencing specifications across vendor datasheets, interface control documents (ICDs), and qualification records before documenting a substitution justification for review. An incorrect substitution on a flight-critical component can cause mission failure, yet the evidence trail behind each decision is often spread across email and undocumented institutional knowledge, so there is no formal, repeatable package for a reviewer to check. A previous post, Manufacturing intelligence with Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings , showed how the model retrieves answers locked inside engineering diagrams, thermal plots, and datasheet charts that text-only pipelines miss. This post picks up where that retrieval work left off, putting those capabilities inside a multi-agent system that assembles substitution evidence, from retrieval to a drafted assessment. In this post, we show how to build a multi-agent engineering assistant that cuts the manual cross-referencing behind part substitution evaluation using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings , and the open source Strands Agents SDK . A planner routes work across three specialist agents that search a multimodal knowledge base, score candidates against deterministic tolerance rules, compare part photos, and ground lifecycle claims in live web data. The engineer remains the decision-maker throughout, because the system assembles evidence and drafts documents without ever approving a substitution on its own. Solution overview The assistant is built around one design rule, which is that the engineer makes every decision and the system assembles the evidence for it. That rule determines where we use large language models (LLMs) and where we use deterministic code instead. Three pillars define the architecture: Deterministic spec-fit evaluation – Tolerance-rule code written in Python scores each candidate part against the reference part and the engineer’s stated requirements. Because the same inputs consistently produce the same pass/flag verdicts, the results can go into a formal engineering review. Multi-agent orchestration – A lightweight planner routes each query to one or more of three specialist agents (Catalog, Evaluation, Knowledge), and a supervisor synthesizes their findings only when more

summary.tldr:
Amazon has introduced a multi-agent engineering assistant architecture designed to automate the evidence-gathering process for aerospace component substitutions. By integrating Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and the open-source Strands Agents SDK, the system aims to replace manual cross-referencing of datasheets, interface control documents (ICDs), and qualification records. The assistant is structured to ensure the human engineer remains the final decision-maker, with the AI responsible for retrieving data, scoring candidates, and drafting assessment documentation.

The architecture relies on a hybrid approach that separates deterministic logic from LLM-based reasoning. A central planner routes tasks to three specialist agents: a Catalog agent for searching, an Evaluation agent for scoring candidates against deterministic Python-based tolerance rules, and a Knowledge agent for grounding lifecycle claims in web data. The system utilizes Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings to extract information from engineering diagrams, thermal plots, and datasheet charts, addressing the limitations of text-only retrieval pipelines. The final output is a formal, repeatable evidence package intended for engineering review, rather than an autonomous decision-making process.
takeaways: **Core Technology Stack:** Utilizes Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings for visual data extraction, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore for orchestration, and the Strands Agents SDK for multi-agent framework.

**Agent Specialization:** The system employs three distinct agents: a Catalog agent for search, an Evaluation agent for deterministic tolerance rule scoring, and a Knowledge agent for external web-based lifecycle verification.
**Deterministic Guardrails:** Engineering tolerance rules are implemented via Python code to ensure consistent, verifiable pass/flag verdicts that meet formal review standards.
**Human-in-the-loop Design:** The system is architected to draft assessments and assemble evidence packages, explicitly prohibiting the AI from approving component substitutions independently.

title: How Circle K accelerated DevOps incident triage to under 15 minutes with Amazon Bedrock
author: Marek Klatowicz
contentSnippet: This post was co-written with Marek Klatowicz, Cloud DevOps Engineer at Circle K. Many DevOps teams know the incident triage pattern: An alert fires, and before anyone can fix the problem, an engineer spends 45–60 minutes figuring out what happened. They pull logs, check service health, and correlate symptoms across a handful of tools. All of this happens before remediation can begin. At Circle K, this challenge scaled with the business. The company operates more than 17,200 convenience and fuel retail stores across 27 countries. Behind the storefronts, a cloud-native infrastructure supports point-of-sale systems, loyalty applications, and electric vehicle (EV) charging applications running on AWS. As the company expanded its digital operations, the triage overhead grew with it. More services meant more alerts, and each one required the same manual investigation before remediation could begin. To address it, Circle K built an automated triage system using Amazon Bedrock , a fully managed service that makes foundation models (FMs) available through a single API. For model availability by AWS Region, refer to Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock . The system uses an agentic AI architecture to investigate each incident autonomously and deliver a structured summary to Slack within minutes of an alert firing. Instead of raw alerts, on-call engineers now receive actionable context, so they can act immediately rather than spending an hour figuring out what happened. Since deploying this system, Circle K has reduced mean triage time to under 15 minutes, a 67–75 percent reduction based on the team’s internal incident-response metrics. In this post, we describe the architecture for both the initial Amazon Bedrock Flows implementation and the migration to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , and share lessons learned from scaling the system. The challenge of triage overhead Circle K’s DevOps team monitors infrastructure across multiple AWS accounts using Grafana. A typical day brings alerts for container restarts, elevated error rates, latency spikes, and failed deployments. Each alert is a useful signal, but as the system expanded, the team wanted to help on-call engineers quickly see which signals needed attention, with the right context. When an alert came in, the triage involved a familiar sequence of manual steps: reviewing recent logs in Amazon CloudWatch , exa

summary.tldr:
Circle K, which manages cloud-native infrastructure for over 17,200 retail locations across 27 countries, has implemented an agentic AI system on Amazon Bedrock to automate DevOps incident triage. By integrating this system into their existing Grafana-based monitoring stack, the company reduced mean incident triage time from 45–60 minutes to under 15 minutes, representing a 67–75 percent efficiency gain. The system replaces manual log correlation and service health checks with an automated process that delivers structured, actionable incident summaries directly to Slack.

The architecture utilizes Amazon Bedrock to provide foundation models via a single API, transitioning from an initial implementation using Amazon Bedrock Flows to the current Amazon Bedrock AgentCore framework. The system autonomously investigates alerts—such as container restarts, latency spikes, and failed deployments—by querying Amazon CloudWatch logs and correlating symptoms across the company's AWS-hosted point-of-sale, loyalty, and EV charging applications. This shift allows on-call engineers to bypass the initial investigative phase and proceed directly to remediation.
takeaways: **Performance Metric:** Mean incident triage time reduced from 45–60 minutes to under 15 minutes.
**Efficiency Gain:** Achieved a 67–75 percent reduction in time spent on manual incident investigation.
**Infrastructure Scale:** Supports cloud-native operations for 17,200+ retail stores across 27 countries.
**Technical Stack:** Utilizes Amazon Bedrock, Amazon CloudWatch, Grafana, and Slack for automated incident reporting.
**Architectural Evolution:** Migrated from Amazon Bedrock Flows to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore for autonomous incident investigation.

title: Raising the quality of insights in agentic analytics
author: MIT Technology Review Insights
contentSnippet: In just a few years, generative AI has changed the face of enterprise analytics, notably by making analytics accessible to users across the organization. Agentic AI promises to do even more, by automating entire workflows and taking actions based on agent insights. But there is a problem: The quality of insights that agents currently generate leaves much to be desired. Fewer than half of agent-generated insights at the organizations surveyed for this report lead to business improvement. And while most respondents praise the quality of their agents’ descriptive insights, reviews of their prescriptive insights—those on which actions are based—are decidedly mixed. DOWNLOAD THE REPORT Failure to produce insights that improve the business deprives organizations of their desired return on investment in agentic analytics. Worse, flawed insights that trigger incorrect actions can cause reputational or financial damage. This report gauges how companies view the quality of the outputs produced by their analytics agents and explores how organizations are seeking to boost insight quality and get their agents working harder for the business. Some key findings from the report include the following: Agentic analytics is only just starting to deliver. On average, 48% of insights generated by analytics agents at the surveyed companies lead to actions that improve the business. That is a marked advance from the 37% average the respondents say generated such actions one year ago. But it means that more than half of the insights generated by analytics agents today are still failing to help businesses. Better quality of insights leads to clear business advantage. At a small cohort of organizations, which we term “insight leaders,” AI agents perform much better than the average. In this group, more than 70% of agent insights lead to actions that improve the business. The insight leaders also give the quality of their agents’ insights higher marks than do the total respondents overall. The quality gap is particularly wide when it comes to prescriptive insights. Insufficient context reduces insight quality. When analytics agents deliver insights of substandard quality, the main reason is a lack of business context, as cited by 55% of surveyed executives.
