title: I built an AI Tamagotchi before Meta could
author: Sean Hollister
contentSnippet: Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta made AI look so stinking cute by giving it a squishy little face — and this holiday season, he wants to sell you a Muse Charm so you can carry your jolly AI helper around like a Tamagotchi. But I won’t be buying one, because we have Muse Charm at home. It cost just $50, and I’ve decided the learning experience was worth it. [Media: https://www.tiktok.com/@verge/video/7702862550014168333] My version doesn’t sport cameras or a 5G cellular radio, but it really talks to Muse and has cute avatars, too! It doubles as a pocket watch and a remote camera viewfinder, and it can (theoretically) control my smart home. Or at least it can if you inject a lot of extra vibe code. Weeks ago, I paid $50 to get a 1.75-inch touchscreen computer pendant drop-shipped from China — specifically the Waveshare ESP32-S3 1.75C. Not only does the push-to-talk AI devkit look a lot like the Muse Charm, but it’s officially sanctioned by Meta. It’s one of the company’s first suggestions if you want to build a “Muse Gadget,” a device that uses Meta’s open-source code and tokens to directly connect to its Muse AI cloud. When the silver metal pocket watch arrived, it felt pretty useless to start. Setup was easy enough — I just plugged it into my PC and pointed Claude at Meta’s GitHub, then paired it to the Muse phone app. But even after I put Meta’s keys on the device, Muse originally thought I was sending it audio clips to transcribe rather than commands. After I cleared that up, Muse’s responses were still slow, and it didn’t answer me out loud. It was hard to tell what it was saying since it only showed a few words onscreen at a time, with no place to read full messages unless I whipped out my phone with its own Muse app. Meta’s build also only came with a single Jolly avatar that mostly just sat there and looked cute, and it wouldn’t automatically discover smart home gadgets like Amazon Echo or Google Home devices do. (This gadget really didn’t do anything useful after my initial install.) And though Meta AI software engineers Anant Narayanan and Jeremy Payne include a neat sample app showing how Muse Gadgets can stream video from your phone camera, the lack of a remote shutter button made it not so useful for taking photos. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/verge-sean-hollister-muse-gadget-331A2570-01-2.jpg?quality=90&strip=all

summary.tldr:
A tech journalist built a custom AI-powered "Tamagotchi" pendant for $50 using the Waveshare ESP32-S3 1.75C developer kit, bypassing Meta's upcoming commercial Muse Charm. The off-the-shelf silver metal pocket watch devkit is officially sanctioned by Meta as a "Muse Gadget" for connecting to Meta's open-source Muse AI cloud. Initial deployment via Meta's GitHub and Claude required significant troubleshooting, as the default build suffered from slow transcription, lacked full message display, featured only a single "Jolly" avatar, and failed to natively discover smart home devices.

Using Claude Code without prior coding experience, the author injected custom "vibe code" to drastically overhaul the hardware's functionality. Modifications included adding a conversation history page, integrating a British ElevenLabs AI voice for text-to-speech output, building a low-quality Bluetooth camera preview, implementing a remote camera shutter for the phone, and creating a multi-tiered Tamagotchi minigame tracking hunger, boredom, sleep, and hygiene. The device was also programmed with a functional three-hand pocket watch face and a local video player running clips of Mark Zuckerberg introducing the Muse Charm, all completed within minutes of natural language prompting.

The author deployed the pendant on a guest Wi-Fi network as a security precaution due to privacy concerns, noting that Meta's servers remain the primary source of latency. The experiment raises questions about whether consumers would be better served by programmable developer kits rather than locked-down commercial hardware like Meta's forthcoming Muse Charm.
takeaways: **Hardware Specifications:** The DIY build used the Waveshare ESP32-S3 1.75C, a 1.75-inch touchscreen computer pendant drop-shipped from China that lacks cameras and a 5G cellular radio.
**Cost & Setup:** The hardware cost $50 and was paired with Meta's open-source Muse AI cloud using code and tokens from Meta's GitHub, facilitated by Claude Code.
**Audio and Voice Modifications:** Default audio responses were upgraded by plugging in a British AI voice from ElevenLabs' free tier and adding a conversation history swipe feature.

**Custom Software Features:** Claude Code added a Tamagotchi minigame with four levels of hunger, boredom, and dirt, a working three-hand pocket watch face built in 15 minutes, a remote phone camera shutter, and a local video player.
**Security Precautions:** The device was placed on a guest Wi-Fi network immediately following reports that Meta's Muse agent leaked a reviewer's home address.

title: Meet Factory Droid 1.0: A Model-Independent Coding Agent Harness Built on Script Mode
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: Factory has released Droid 1.0 , the largest update yet to the Factory Droid agent harness. The main change is programmatic tool calling, now on by default. The model writes a program that runs its tools. One model request can now drive hundreds of tool calls. TL;DR Size: Base prompt is 13,055 input tokens, down 37% from 20,887. Only 2 tool definitions ship up front, down from 11. Runs on: macOS and Windows desktop app, a terminal UI, and the Node SDK @factory/droid-sdk . Works with any supported model, including your own API keys. Performance: Highest pass rate of every harness Factory tested, on the same model, at lower cost. Best: 65.2% on Terminal-Bench 4 with Claude Opus 5.5, at $4.73 per passed task (self-reported). Worst: With GPT-6.1 Sol, Droid takes 10% longer per passed task than Codex. What is Droid 1.0? Droid 1.0 is a model-independent coding agent harness from Factory. Factory defines a harness as everything around the model. That means the prompts, the tools, how tool results return, and the loop . Users pick a model or let Factory Router choose a cost-efficient mix. How does programmatic tool calling work? In a standard loop, every tool output lands in the model’s context. With programmatic tool calling (PTC), the model writes a program instead. Droid implements this as a Script tool . The model writes JavaScript that runs in a sandbox. The sandbox has no file, network, or system access of its own. Raw files, search results, and logs stay inside the program. Only printed output returns to the model. Independent calls run concurrently. The idea builds on CodeAct (Wang et al., 2024) . Factory reports these results from its own sessions: Unit test fix: 15 tool calls took 5 model calls instead of 10. The task finished in 41.6 s instead of 56.8 s. Linear cleanup: 151 issues moved and verified in 312 tool calls. The Script used 2 requests and about 61,000 tokens. Factory models direct calls at 36 requests and about 3.1M tokens. CI sweep: 5,384 jobs across 547 runs, in 2 requests. Under 0.1% of tool results reached the model’s context. On Claude Opus 5.5, Script mode cuts Droid’s cost by 15% versus direct tool calling. It is on by default for 10 models, including GPT-6.1 Sol and Kimi K3. <iframe id="fdx-frame" title="Factory Droid 1.0 interactive explainer" style="width:100%;height:600px;border:0;display:block;" loading="lazy" srcdoc="<!doctype html>

One model request can now drive hundreds of tool calls. TL;DR Size: Base prompt is 13,055 input tokens, down 37% from 20,887. Only 2 tool definitions ship up front, down from 11.

Works with any supported model, including your own API keys.

title: Vercel Labs Open-Sources agent-desktop for Agent Computer Use
author: Michal Sutter
contentSnippet: Vercel Labs has released agent-desktop , an open-source CLI for AI agent computer use on macOS, Windows and Linux. agent-desktop reads each app through the operating system’s accessibility tree, not through screenshots. An agent gets a JSON snapshot with a ref for every element it can act on. Version 1.0.2 shipped on October 30, 2026, under Apache-2.0. For developers, any shell-capable coding agent can now drive native apps without a vision model. TL;DR Library: Rust CLI and a C library. 60 command names, 56 operational . Runs on: macOS 13+, Windows 10 1809+ or Server 2019+, Ubuntu 24.04+ , on x64 and ARM64. Plain CPU, no GPU. Performance: Deterministic, retry-safe ref actions. No independent computer-use benchmark yet. Best: 78% to 96% fewer tokens on dense Electron apps via skeleton traversal ( self-reported ). What is agent-desktop? agent-desktop is a Rust CLI and C library from Vercel Labs for reading and operating desktop apps. It is a tool that agents call, not an agent . It embeds no LLM and has no GUI. Every command prints one JSON envelope and exits. The observe, act and verify loop stays in your agent. How does agent-desktop work? Each command flows through a fixed chain. The CLI or C library calls agent-desktop-core , which reaches the OS only through a PlatformAdapter trait. One platform crate then talks to the native accessibility API: macOS: AX API Windows: UI Automation Linux: AT-SPI Core never imports a platform crate. Each binary is compiled to drive exactly one OS. Snapshots and refs A snapshot assigns qualified refs such as @s8f3k2p9:e8 . The snapshot ID inside the ref makes it self-describing. A bare @e8 is rejected with INVALID_ARGS . When the UI changes, an action returns STALE_REF or AMBIGUOUS_TARGET . The agent then takes a fresh snapshot. Every error carries a disposition . Agents should retry only when it says safe . Ref resolution is strict and fails closed rather than guessing. Skeleton and drill-down Dense apps can expose thousands of accessibility nodes. A --skeleton snapshot reads only 3 levels deep . Cut containers report a children_count and get a drill ref. snapshot --root then reads one region into the same snapshot. The builder reported a 78% to 96% token cut versus full-tree dumps in Slack, VS Code and Notion. In Apple Maps, he reported 3,811 tokens per look falling to 273 . A simulated 52-step task dropped from 198k to 3

Version 1.0.2 shipped on October 30, 2026, under Apache-2.0. For developers, any shell-capable coding agent can now drive native apps without a vision model. TL;DR Library: Rust CLI and a C library.

title: Decision-Centric Research: A Calibrated Decision Model and Benchmark for Scientific Agents
author: Shaoning Zeng
contentSnippet: Scientific agents make consequential choices about evidence, next actions and research strategy, but choices embedded in generated text are difficult to evaluate independently. Decision-Centric Research (DCR) is introduced to make individual choices the common unit of supervision, prediction and evaluation through typed predictions over an explicit Research State. DCR defines 24 decision types, ten of which are instantiated in the Research Decision Benchmark (RD-Bench) of 2,000 rule-generated cases. The Decision-Centric Research Model (DCRM) shares a candidate-token readout across types to produce answers and option probabilities in one forward pass. Under a held-out research-domain split, a 0.6B DCRM (state-aware) achieves 89.4% Top-1 accuracy, compared with 27.8% for DCRM (question-only) trained with the same recipe and 36.4% for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. All 30 type-seed comparisons against DCRM (question-only) are significant after Holm correction. After held-out calibration, the resulting prediction sets contain a mean of 1.515 candidates at 97.1% empirical label coverage, reducing mean set size by 57.4% relative to DCRM (question-only) at similar coverage. These results establish a compact state-aware decision layer with accurate typed prediction and an inspectable uncertainty interface.

These results establish a compact state-aware decision layer with accurate typed prediction and an inspectable uncertainty interface.
